rows.text: TE28 Area C:West Layer 3a faunal remains included Neotoma sp. (MNI 1–2), Dipodomys sp. (MNI 1), and tentatively Neotomodon alstoni (MNI 1). Bones showed no burning, roasting, or other cultural modification. Griffiths interpreted them as likely intrusive rodents rather than deliberate offerings.

Cave TE28 Area C:West Layer 5f contained a burrow beneath Rock 2 tapering toward the former Blockage 12. Small find 40 comprised at least 81 animal-bone fragments later assessed from photographs rather than direct reexamination of specimens.

Cave TE28 Area C:West Layer 3a fire pit near Blockage 12 contained a semicircular burnt shell and fish-bone concentration 25 × 35 cm (small finds 23–25). Sload interprets the feature as possibly linked to closure, not securely to pyramid construction.

Sload (2007) defines Teotihuacan concrete as a mixture of crushed volcanic scoria (cascajo) and mud mortar, attributing the term to Millon (1973:27). Sload reports its use as cave floor covering and facing on constructed narrowings.

The cave entrance involved a vertical descent of roughly 6–7 m. Four narrowed passages in the western portion could be traversed only singly while bending; three passages preserve at least two architectural modification phases, one involving a concrete facing. The eastern section was partitioned by approximately 17–19 full-height masonry blockages.

Drain stones, stone covers and silt marks suggest that the presently dry cave encountered or managed water during antiquity. Millon and Altschul proposed that water was brought in from outside; Manzanilla proposed possible seepage from surrounding terrain. None demonstrated an internal spring.

Before the 1978 archaeological tests, cave blockages had already been breached in their upper portions, and INAH interventions between 1971 and 1976 replaced a damaged rock-cut stairway with a metal staircase, installed electricity, opened blockages and removed substantial rubble, including from the four-chambered terminus. Hence original deposits and later cleared areas cannot automatically be treated as intact ancient strata.

In two Area A pits measuring 1 × 1.25 m each, excavators recovered only six of TE28’s 273 sherds. Three charcoal samples beneath intact concrete included early Beta 220743 (1930±40 BP; 95% calibrated 10 BCE–140 CE), early Beta 220744 (1970±40 BP; 95% 50 BCE–110 CE), and later Beta 220745 (1830±40 BP; 95% 90–260 CE). Sload interprets this combination as compatible with infrequent activity before a later concrete floor.

Area B west excavation exposed a posthole and adjacent charcoal deposits. Beta 220747 occurred in the bright-yellow crushed-tepetate layer (95% calibrated 20–220 CE); Beta 220749 and 220750 came from the posthole (95% ranges 110–330 CE and 60–240 CE respectively). Sload observed that Area B lacked the concrete floor seen elsewhere, and proposed that stacked basalt slabs from the terminus may formerly have served as flooring.

The 2007 radiocarbon report classified archaeological charcoal into ash-bearing fire pits, ashless compact concentrations, and isolated pieces. These contexts differ in their ability to date in-situ burning. The reported calibration intervals were computed for the published analysis, so comparing them numerically with later Bayesian posterior ranges requires accounting for recalibration and the changing selected sample populations.

In a bulk preliminary sorting of 37,746 pottery fragments from Front C of the Sun Pyramid, excavators identified 35,736 (94.7%) as Tzacualli, 1,985 (5.2%) as Patlachique, 23 (0.1%) as Miccaotli and two as Cuanalán. The pottery-date majority favors an earlier ceramic-relative chronology than the excavators’ later radiocarbon-based construction estimate.

Two separate charcoal determinations PPS-1 (Beta-277972, 1780±40 BP; 1σ 220–260 and 290–320 CE) and PPS-2 (Beta-277973, 1820±40 BP; 1σ 130–240 CE) were taken from a carbon concentration burned in place above Floor 2 in Pits 29 and 27. They date burning of sampled wood, not by themselves the initial excavation or deposition of every surrounding floor.

PPS-7 (Beta-277978, 1900±40 BP) came from an ash-rich layer beneath the floor of Structure 1 in Pit 6, yielding 1σ 60–130 CE. It is the earliest of the Sun Pyramid Project sample series and accords more closely with Tzacualli ceramic chronology. Sugiyama and colleagues consider the ash possibly redeposited or from a pre-Structure 1 context, limiting its value for dating the main building; Sload argues the authors’ construction model retains this excluded sample.

The 2013 excavation reports PPS-5 (Beta-277976; 1820±40 BP; 1σ 130–240 CE) from tibia of Burial 4 in Pits 22–23 and PPS-6 (Beta-277977; 1760±40 BP; 1σ 230–330 CE) from a probable tibia of Burial 2 in Pit 17. Burial 4 was a child aged approximately four to six; Burial 2 was a perinatal infant located near bedrock west of Structure 1. Direct bone dates establish sampled individuals’ radiocarbon age, while the precise relationship of Burial 4 to Structure 1 was not observed stratigraphically.

PPS-3 (Beta-277974; 2150±50 radiocarbon BP) dates a conch-shell fragment placed with Offering 1 in Tunnel 2 within the pyramid fill; its publication-calibrated 1σ range is 140–260 CE. The investigators used the Marine04 curve for this shell, distinct from the terrestrial IntCal04 curve used for other samples. The offering also contained obsidian blades, projectile points, pyrite, organic materials and an anthropomorphic obsidian figurine.

PPS-4 (Beta-277975, 1700±40 BP; 1σ 260–290 and 320–400 CE) came from uncharred wood in a posthole at Pit 9, on bedrock approximately 80 m into the west–east archaeological tunnel. The wood was submerged and highly degraded; excavation authors suggested possible contamination by water and treated the anomalously late age with caution.

The only newly obtained Sun Pyramid Project date from the subterranean tunnel was PPS-8 (Beta-277979; 1870±40 BP, 1σ 80–210 CE). It came from carbon fragments in the nucleus of the entrance talud at Front D/Pit 1. The authors considered it evidence for construction of entrance architecture before or roughly contemporaneous with the main pyramid.

Sugiyama et al. 2013 Table 3 reproduces 16 earlier cave dates and their new PPS-8. Their OxCal model retains seven TMP results classed as postholes or fire pits (Beta-220749, -220750, -220753, -220758, -208984, -220763 and -220764), yielding a modeled 1σ interval roughly 139–240 CE. Nine other TMP dates, largely from fill, were not incorporated. Sload’s subsequent interpretation separates cave excavation, use, and termination, questioning whether these seven samples date a single construction event.

Sload reports Barba Pingarrón and Córdova Frunz’s geological reconstruction that Teotihuacan quarrying targeted loose volcanic scoria (cascajo) beneath a hard, consolidated tepetate/tuff layer: once extracted, quarry roofs were intentionally collapsed. They interpret a network of linear depressions and tunnels as construction-material procurement, not necessarily ritual chambers.

Linda Manzanilla interpreted the Sun Pyramid cave as an original quarry that later acquired ritual status; Sload objects that cave pottery predates much of the Classic-period mining network, that its layout is unlike quarry tunnels, and that the cave’s end chambers and axial position suggest deliberate independent design. These are competing explanations for the cave’s initial function, not an excavated agreement.

Sload maps the Sun Pyramid cave on the main east–west centerline of the monument. She states that the two transverse cave chambers align with the junction of the pyramid and the later adosada platform, while the four-room terminus corresponds to the summit position of the pyramid before addition of its reconstructed fourth and fifth tiers. These correlations form part of her argument for deliberate design.

Sload describes a second artificial cave under the Feathered Serpent Pyramid at the Ciudadela, with a west-to-east passage beneath its principal staircase and side chambers near the junction with the adjoining platform; she uses its engineered axial placement to argue that mountain-cave relationships were spatially intentional at more than one monument.

Sload distinguishes seven reported radiocarbon samples taken within the Sun Pyramid along the Noguera tunnel: PPS-7 came from an ash lens in the pyramid fill and agreed with Tzacualli ceramic dating, while PPS-1 through PPS-6 came from features placed at ground level on the monument’s east–west centerline; the latter cluster later and their 68% calibrated ranges do not overlap PPS-7. The event represented by the later cluster remains disputed.

Sload argues that Sugiyama et al. included PPS-7 in a Bayesian model that yielded a 170–310 CE construction interval but discounted PPS-7 in their narrative interpretation; she contends that dropping it and rerunning the model would change the reported interval. This is a published methodological criticism, not a demonstrated recalculation undertaken in this batch.

Sload describes a concrete-covered floor and wall segment labeled Structure 1, buried within the pyramid. She reports that the 2013 excavation team classified it as preceding the main pyramid, while she considers a later insertion plausible because Structure 1 is oriented to Teotihuacan north and aligns with the reconstructed summit of the later, enlarged pyramid.

A 1977 photograph reproduced as Sload Figure 2.7 shows the surviving original north corner of the adosada-platform stair relative to the metal door of the cave entrance; small stones embedded in cement identify an INAH reconstruction. Thus not all masonry visible at this entrance represents an untouched Teotihuacan building surface.

Sload records the hypothesis that a principal tomb once occupied the four-chambered cave terminus and subsequent stone blockages created burial chambers. She objects that no positive grave context has been identified and that invoking complete prehistoric looting is an unverified explanation for the missing physical evidence. This challenges, but does not conclusively exclude, funerary use.

In the Sun Pyramid cave, Sload probed both sides of the existing passage at 50-cm horizontal intervals and at three vertical heights. Probe depths indicated up to 1–3 m of additional hollow space behind parts of the present rock facings, reaching 2.95 m behind the south wall near Station 5 at 1.18 m above the floor. Area C excavation found the excavated cave wall over 1 m behind its northern stacked-rock wall and 2 m behind its southern stacked-rock wall.

At the southern transverse chamber (TE 28 Area A, South pit), excavators recorded charcoal band C several centimeters under a concrete floor; the band extended about 17 cm into the underlying cascajo fill. Some charcoal lumps reached roughly 5 cm diameter, but the excavators noted neither ash nor heat discoloration of the surrounding cascajo. Sample Beta 220745 came from this band.

At TE 28 Area D near the west entrance, a transverse ancient step crossed the cave passage. Excavators found the Teotihuacan concrete floor ending immediately at the step and a few centimeters above its base, without extending beneath it. The overlying cascajo layers thickened toward the east and thinned approaching the step. These relationships indicate that the step was present before the final concrete floor was laid.

Area D contained a modern packed-earth surface above a Teotihuacan concrete floor. Below that sealing surface lay distinguishable deposits including a northeast–southwest oriented fire pit (Layer 3, charcoal sample Beta 220763), cascajo fill (Layer 3b, charcoal Beta 220764), a packed earth floor (Layer 3c), and crushed yellow tepetate (BYCT) grading into initial cascajo fill (Layer 4/5 in Sload reconstruction). The northwestern silt deposits were interpreted by excavators as evidence of repeated water entry.

At Sload’s 2006 reassessment of the 1978 TE 28 collections, she could not locate four small worked/unworked shell finds, one mica fragment, and three worked obsidian items from the terminus contexts; she reports none of the 12 TE28 obsidian pieces could be located. Obsidian from an independent 1977 surface collection was present. The unavailable materials restrict subsequent compositional or use-wear analysis.

From the cave’s terminal area, TE28 documented both unworked/minimally modified slate retaining embedded pyrite crystal impressions and a slate fragment with a retouched edge and furrowing. Sload’s illustrated examples distinguish one from INAH backfill in pit B:East from another in the brighter yellow crushed-tepetate (BYCT) layer of B:West. Their distinct proveniences prevent treating both as undisturbed ritual offerings.

An illustrated cleaved slate fragment from the terminus has a drilled hole and secondary mineralization on both faces; Sload notes that known Teotihuacan mirror backings usually carry tesserae on only one face and therefore treats identification as a possible mirror backing rather than secure. Another three-straight-sided slate piece from B:NE has a polygonal form and possible jarosite on its surface; a pendant function is suggested by its outline and hole position, not demonstrated by an in-situ attachment.

Earlier INAH work in the four-chambered cave terminus reportedly removed and stacked hundreds of basalt lajas (stone slabs) of varied sizes. During later mapping, Millon recorded slab locations and TE28 found no concrete floor in Area B. Sload interprets the slabs and shallow stratigraphy as possible remnants of a slab floor dismantled before cave closure.

Braswell documents Chicanel-phase pottery made in the Maya region mixed with Tzacualli ceramics in Sun Pyramid fill, but no Maya Early Classic polychromes of a type dated to after about 150 CE in those reported contexts. He cautions that these are redeposited (tertiary) fill assemblages, so their absence cannot conclusively exclude a Sun Pyramid construction date later than 150 CE.

The assemblages from Kaminaljuyu Mounds A and B in Guatemala included Teotihuacan Xolalpan pottery alongside Early Classic Maya lowland polychromes, as documented by Kidder, Jennings, and Shook (1946). Braswell explains that ceramic comparisons with Holmul and Uaxactun, where inscriptions helped date analogous polychromes, originally supplied an external chronological anchor for Teotihuacan Xolalpan.

Braswell reports that Xolalpan ceramics were found at Tikal in the 1960s in Early Classic archaeological contexts with direct, stratigraphic, or iconographic associations to dated Maya hieroglyphic texts. Such cross-dated finds are independent of Sun Pyramid fill and must be considered before shifting the absolute ages of Teotihuacan ceramic phases.

Braswell distinguishes evidence for earlier Teotihuacan contacts in the Maya area during Miccaotli or Early Tlamimilolpa from the better-attested interaction pulse beginning with the Maya calendar event 11 Eb’ 15 Mak in 378 CE. He places the latter major interaction through approximately 450 CE, and argues that a wholesale later redating could compress the two contact pulses into the fourth and early fifth centuries.

Braswell identifies concrete consequences of moving Teotihuacan ceramic phases later by about a century: Tikal Manik 1–2 and Uaxactun Tzakol 1–2 ceramic sequences, as well as architectural chronologies at Tikal and Kaminaljuyu, would have to be reassessed. He emphasizes that Maya Long Count inscriptions supply independent chronological constraints and that a Teotihuacan reinterpretation should not be extrapolated across these sequences without evaluating their independent dates.

Beramendi-Orosco and colleagues modeled 33 radiocarbon determinations from Teopancazco in four stratigraphic groups: Tlamimilolpa, its transition to Early Xolalpan, Early Xolalpan, and Late Xolalpan. Five samples were charred roof beams or columns; the remainder were from hearths and activity areas. Two anomalously ancient determinations, Beta-180340 and Beta-180337, each 2460±40 14C BP, were traced to altered contexts and identified as statistical outliers; Beta-180337 was suspected of disturbance during Batres’s 1884 excavations.

Beramendi-Orosco and colleagues anchored their Teopancazco Bayesian model against archaeomagnetic dates from burned lime plaster: c. 350±25 CE for termination-related flooring and c. 550±25 CE for the major fire affecting Xalla and Teopancazco. The agreement was used to test whether modeled radiocarbon phase boundaries were plausible. The 350 and 550 CE figures are dates of particular sampled thermal events, not direct dates for first construction of the Sun Pyramid.

Removing two disturbed-context radiocarbon values from the 33-determination Teopancazco model shifted posterior boundaries later and changed calibrated intervals: model B dates were about 12% wider on average than model A; the estimated end of Late Xolalpan moved to approximately 450–580 CE, compatible with an archaeomagnetic large-fire marker at c. 550±25 CE. The same study found that a third model with different phase-boundary constraints gave intervals averaging 4.7% wider than model B. This is an empirical example of why source selection and prior assumptions must be documented, not an independent rerun of the Sun Pyramid model.

In Figure 8.13, Sload illustrates two sherds interpreted as parts of Tlaloc-type jars: one 5.7 g fragment recovered in an undisturbed earthen floor deposit at the cave entrance, with paste assigned to Miccaotli or Early Tlamimilolpa, and a separate 5.4 g fragment from Tract 2 of the 1977 surface collection. She compares their profiles with a Miccaotli jar photographed at the Museo Nacional de Antropología. The two recovery contexts must not be merged into one sealed offering.

Sload reports no comales, composite theatre-type censers, candeleros, Copa ware, Copoid ware, cylindrical vases with or without nubbin supports, or polychrome or resist-painted vessels in the mapped cave collections. Fine matte ware was limited to a tiny disturbed-context miniature fragment in Area C; a dense-ware bowl fragment occurred only in Tract 6 of the 1977 surface collection. These absences support her assignment of the principal cave ceramic assemblage to Tzacualli–Early Tlamimilolpa but cannot alone rule out later visits or prove that no such objects were used.

Sload interprets the low number of sherds in undisturbed deposits, the mixing of ceramic phases, and the preponderance of small fragments as possible evidence for repeated removal of materials through sweeping during cave use and closure. She explicitly acknowledges that the sherd-size impression is unconfirmed and that statistical representativeness cannot be established. No archaeological sweep marks or securely dated sweep deposits are reported in these passages; the hypothesis cannot be promoted to an observed ancient practice.

Sarabia describes the Pyramid of the Sun as the center of a walled ceremonial complex measuring roughly 350–400 m per side. Its enclosing platform is reported as 6 m high and 35 m thick; it enclosed the pyramid, a frontal plaza, and residential structures north of that plaza. The main approach was a broad western staircase linking the plaza to the Avenue of the Dead. The compound, not just the pyramid, was the urban planning unit.

Sarabia inventories 16 research tunnel entries through the Sun Pyramid, totaling 376.20 m of excavation length. His table distinguishes Gamio’s 97 m east-side tunnel (1917–1918), Pérez and Noguera’s 116 m west-side tunnel (1933), and several shorter later investigations. A 6 m ramp connected the two principal excavations into a 219 m east–west route. These excavations were made by archaeologists, not ancient Teotihuacanos.

The 1933 Pérez–Noguera tunnel extended 116 m from the west facade on the pyramid’s east–west axis but remained about 1.5 m above the natural tepetate/rock surface. From 2008 to 2011, researchers excavated 59 test pits from its floor down to the ancient basal level and three short auxiliary tunnels, recovering buried architectural and ritual deposits that earlier exploration could not observe. This is a documented sampling-position effect, not proof that all unexcavated sectors contain similar offerings.

Later foundation excavations revealed plaster/mortar floors and a wall approximately 2 m thick and more than 14 m long along a north–south axis; Sarabia reports that two earlier architectural structures were almost entirely dismantled to establish the later pyramid foundation. The overall original floor plan and function cannot securely be reconstructed.

Sarabia describes the monumental core as stratified deposits of soil, sand and crushed tepetate containing ceramic fragments, obsidian and charcoal, with no substantial organized adobe-block system and no large stone mass in the central fill. He distinguishes this fill from the later protective stone facing and the heavier construction of subsequent additions. The sampled interior is not evidence that no stone was used anywhere in the monument.

The excavators report a fetal individual (designated Burial 2) from a level older than a pre-pyramid substructure; a separate child aged about four to six years, with cranial modification, was deposited in a small pit near that pre-pyramid structure when the main pyramid was built. Their distinct stratigraphic contexts preclude treating the two remains as one burial event. Ritual killing is suggested by the authors but is not independently proven by the recorded placement alone.

The authors place Offering 1 in fill that sealed the intentionally destroyed pre-pyramid substructure. The assemblage included worked obsidian blades, projectile points and figurines, a pyrite disk, a large marine shell and organic fragments; it appears to have been deposited and immediately covered as the core was raised. Its stratigraphic position differs from the square bedrock-level pit that held Offering 2.

Offering 2 was placed in a square 1.75 × 1.75 m pit excavated down to tepetate. The authors enumerate obsidian prismatic blades, miniatures, points and an anthropomorphic image, three pyrite–slate disks plus an L-shaped object, 11 storm-deity vessels, two complete greenstone figurines and a greenstone mask, a marine shell and eight smaller shells, a puma skull/claws, wolf skull, condor remains and an entire eagle with evidence that it ate two rabbits. Thin wooden pieces were arranged on east–west and north–south axes. Its location was apparently keyed to the earlier underground passage rather than exactly the pyramid center.

Sarabia reports an enlargement approximately 6 m thick on the north, east and south faces, apparently limited to the lowest two pyramid bodies. It used steps of stone-and-mud masonry enclosing tezontle fill, abutting the older pyramid slope. Possible drivers include architectural stabilization or political and ceremonial redesign; he does not claim a settled motive.

Along this subsequent expansion, Sarabia recorded a surrounding bench about 3 m wide by 0.60 m high, sloping markedly outward, accompanied by a channel. The channel runs around the monument and directs rainwater toward the southeast corner; natural rock is exposed at its bottom. The physical drainage arrangement is documented, but whether it was the principal motive for all remodeling remains unestablished.

Two short tunnels in the adosada platforms, plus stratigraphic cuts in the central and southern sections, led Sarabia to infer at least four building phases. Architectural fragments suggest sculptural programs showing processions of felines, and the author compares the imagery to felids and coyotes in murals from Atetelco and Tetitla. These are reconstructions from fragments; the full original sculptural program is not intact and cannot be described as wholly observable today.

Sarabia distinguishes the adosada construction from the largely earthen main-pyramid core: adosada platforms used tezontle and basalt stones joined with mud to create solid support for heavy andesite and basalt sculptures. The construction-material distinction provides physical evidence that the platforms were not simply part of the earliest mass fill.

Sarabia summarizes geophysical survey and archaeological work identifying tunnels north/east of the city originally excavated to obtain construction material. Investigations associated with Linda Manzanilla found later post-Teotihuacan domestic, storage and ritual use in four east-side tunnels. The article also points to Gamio’s early-twentieth-century record of Indigenous residents living in modified ancient tunnels. These are not the same structures or time period as the purposeful ceremonial passage beneath the Sun Pyramid.

In 1992–1994 a 24 m tunnel opened on the northern face collapsed and was abandoned; the vertical opening was consolidated in 2009 partly because rainwater collected and ran down it. Sarabia records major deterioration of reinforced-concrete tunnel supports, including about 300 columns along a 215 m sector, because they were seated in damp compressed pyramid fill rather than bedrock, which lay about 1.20–2.10 m below. Steel rails installed in 2010 stabilized several of the most damaged sections. Modern interventions therefore alter the physical contexts that later investigators inspect.

Sarabia distinguishes the 103 m ancient passage beneath the Sun Pyramid, accessed by a shaft approximately 6.5 m deep, from the similarly long but approximately 14 m deep passage cut through tepetate beneath the Ciudadela and Feathered Serpent Temple complex. The first was excavated in basaltic bedrock; the latter in consolidated tepetate. These specific passages are not the later archaeological research tunnels excavated through building fill.

The 2014 authors give a west Noguera tunnel finding of one unusually thick north–south wall with a 2 m section and more than 14 m preserved length, showing a talud slope on both faces coupled with vertical masonry. The structure was deliberately destroyed during later pyramid construction; its proposed public function remains inferential.

Sarabia’s later overview places original construction between the first and second centuries CE (p.47) and elsewhere describes the original core as Miccaotli/Early Tlamimilolpa with a later phase enlargement. The 2014 joint-authored publication instead suggests around 240 CE, while the 2013 joint article abstract gives a modeled 170–310 CE interval. These are incompatible unless phase conventions, modeled intervals, and specific construction events are explicitly reconciled. Do not publish a unique accepted construction date.

The 2013 excavation-team abstract hypothesizes royal burials or ritual offerings in the underground tunnel; the 2014 authors’ excerpt also proposes a possible burial of a supreme leader. In the later 2022 report Sarabia concludes that deposits under monumental centers are dedicatory offerings rather than formal tombs, even where human remains occur. Disagreement in interpretation should not be silently reconciled as confirmation of a royal tomb.

Sload reports that Baker et al. (1974) mapped 19 alleged blockage locations in the eastern passage, but review by Drewitt, Millon, Altschul, and Sload found neither mortar nor concrete at the locations marked for Blockages 1 and 19. Sload therefore treats 17 blockages as confirmed, while noting that new fieldwork would be needed for a definitive count.

At Blockage 10, the west-face concrete merges with the floor immediately to the west; at Blockage 11 the floor continues westward but does not extend below the former footprint of the blockage. Sload interprets the repeated building pattern as installing a stone-and-mud blockage, facing its west side with concrete and continuing that concrete as a floor toward the next planned blockage. This implies a closing sequence progressing from the eastern terminus toward the western entrance.

Sload reports C. Earle Smith’s microscopic identification of sedge in a wattle-and-daub fragment from inside Blockage 11 (C:East SF 20). The plant material had been mineral-replaced by gypsum. Drewitt also noted plant remnants in the south-side mortar at Blockage 2. These observations support the use of plant-containing mud mortar in at least some closure walls but do not independently date their construction.

In TE28’s macrobotanical examination, Table 4.1 lists 224 identified pieces and 1,169 unidentified pieces across 404.5 liters of soil. Sload reports 99.5% uncarbonized material and identifies Conyza, Jaltomata and Physalis as the commonest identified genera; she argues that relatively uniform low-density botanical material across fill and use layers favors matrices gathered locally rather than reused construction refuse. The material-source conclusion is an interpretation.

Sload 2020 Table 4.1 reports 911 macrobotanical specimens across 225 L in Area C (Blockages 11–12) versus 33 specimens across 49.5 L in Area D (cave entrance); these represent assemblage counts and do not identify ritual offerings.

Sload 2020 Table 4.1 reports undisturbed fill: 506 macrobotanical pieces in 168.75 L (3.0/L); undisturbed use: 490 pieces in 105 L (4.67/L). Overall recovery is 1393 pieces and 404.5 L, leaving 397 pieces and 130.75 L outside the undisturbed fill/use subset. These are recovery measurements, not proof of ancient diet or offerings.

University of Pittsburgh 2020 Sun Pyramid cave botanical codebook explicitly exemplifies registro 050500, TE28B West pit layer 1, with one uncarbonized Argemone (Papaveraceae), and registro 050565, TE28D layer 5, with one uncarbonized Oxalis (Oxalidaceae), 10 L soil floated per registro. Codebook examples only, not full specimen dataset; no ancient dietary or ceremonial interpretation warranted.

Sload reports Beta 208984 1920 ± 60 BP, calibrated 1σ 30–130 CE, 2σ 40 BCE–230 CE, from an apparent fire pit by Rock 1 on early fill. She interprets charcoal as early Use, not direct Sun Pyramid construction dating.

Beta 220753 (C:East layer 4d fire pit, 1810 ± 40 BP, 2σ 110–330 CE) lies farther south of Figure 5.1's projected cross-section. Author notes pit oriented roughly 90 degrees to section; drawing cannot establish direct superposition between Beta 220754 and 208984.

Sload reran an OxCal overlapping-phase model with Beta 220760 and 220745 moved from Termination to Use. Modeled excavation onset barely changed; Use extended later, while Termination posterior had a second near-mid-fourth-century mode nearly as strong as mid-third-century one.

The most recent cave charcoal sample Beta 266130 from C:West layer 5h below Blockage 12 yielded 1700 ± 40 BP (2σ 240–420 CE); Sload reports an individual agreement index of 57.7, below the discussed 60% threshold.

Torras Freixa reports earth mixed with tepetate volcanic tuff in the Sun Pyramid core, containing ceramics, lithic artifacts and charcoal. She cites botanical evidence indicating that some of this construction earth had previously been agricultural soil; prior agricultural use is a reported interpretation, not established direct excavation evidence from this source inspection.

In TE28's undisturbed Area D fire-pit deposit associated with radiocarbon sample Beta 220763, excavators recovered a flower-pot-type censer rim/body fragment reported to weigh 68.1 g and to bear a post-firing whitewash with fugitive cinnabar-red paint. Sload identifies it as a Tzacualli–Miccaotli or possibly Miccaotli–Early Tlamimilolpa example; the charcoal date pertains to the deposit, not directly to the manufacture of the vessel.

Sload documents magnetite fragments from a bright-yellow crushed-tepetate (BYCT) layer in TE28 Area B:West and a gypsum specimen from INAH backfill in Area B:East, illustrated in Figure 8.5. Field identification of the magnetite was followed by S. Davidovits' magnet test in the laboratory in 2009. Figure 8.5 also depicts a green stone with incised lines on its polished face. The differing contexts must be maintained: backfill specimens cannot be assigned to an undisturbed original placement.

Among 18 ceramic pieces considered for later Teotihuacan activity, 17 were nonphaseable and one was assigned to Xolalpan; none was assigned to Metepec. Four 1977 surface finds from entrance Tracts 10 and 11 consist of one Xolalpan olla, one Regular Thin Orange, one Coarse Thin Orange and one San Martín Orange sherd.
A 0.6 g rim sherd from TE28 Area C:West Layer 5f rodent burrow has a black rim, polished red exterior and dark-cored fine paste, described as resembling an Aztec black-on-red bowl.

The Second Narrowing has a concrete-coated middle section with two non-concrete-faced extensions. At its west end, a concrete floor continues beneath the masonry extension and concrete on the cave wall extends behind it, documenting an architectural sequence.

Laja Passage has an eastern concrete-faced section and western mud-mortared stone section. The publication reports Drewitt's excavation of an intact 15 cm wide concrete floor strip at its east end, and three finger impressions in mud mortar above the western entrance.

The single-section Fourth Narrowing lacks concrete facing but its masonry covers concrete at the entrance of the South Transverse Chamber; a laja roof is reported. This shows masonry superposition consistent with later modification of the passage.

The 2007 laboratory report recorded 978 faunal fragments in two analyzed samples: 969 in TE28:C fire pit and 9 in TE28:B SF15. At least 513 shell fragments were recorded, of which 504 were shorter than 5 mm; columella fragments suggested 3 to 5 individual snails. These numbers describe the analyzed samples only.

Griffitts reports that shell fragments could be Sonorella (terrestrial) or Helisoma (freshwater), which cannot be securely distinguished; fish bone recorded by excavators was no longer available for the 2007 examination. Human transport in fish or attached vegetation and rodent transport remain hypothetical pathways.

The faunal analyst identified only three blackened rodent-sized fragments, which might reflect heat or mineral staining. She observed no other clear burning or cultural modifications in the analyzed bone and shell and judged identified rodents likely intrusive.

In a letter to Jorge Acosta dated 29 July 1974, Doris Heyden stated that the cave appeared after ground subsidence during heavy rains in autumn 1971, interpreted it as a natural grotto, and proposed an ancient stream and sanctuary based partly on stone drain tubes and covers. This documents her 1974 interpretation, not established cave geology or ritual history.

Sload 2007 Figure 10 places Beta 220747 partly in the BYCT layer toward the southeast of Area B:West, whereas Beta 220749 and Beta 220750 cluster in the posthole. Beta 220750 is below Beta 220749. Table 2 gives calibrated 2-sigma intervals of 20–220 CE for 220747, 110–330 CE for 220749 and 60–240 CE for 220750. The dates overlap and their calibration intercepts do not establish separate exact post-use dates.

Sload 2020 describes SF31 in Area C:West as a circular concentration of burnt iridescent shell approximately 20 cm in diameter and 2 cm thick, with charcoal but no ash, in Layer 4d at the upper surface of BYCT Layer 4e and below Layer 3. She reports alignment with the east edge of Blockage 12 and west edge of Rock 2, but ritual significance is a hypothesis.

In the South Transverse Chamber, excavators reported several large, harder stones unlike the smaller rocks embedded in the surrounding matrix. Altschul and Drewitt excavated underneath to check whether the stones were bedrock or fill, finding the stones resting on soil rather than embedded. No equivalent deliberately placed stones were reported in the North pit. The suggestion that the chamber was additionally hollowed out to place them is an inference.

At the western cave entrance, Area D excavations showed a concrete floor that reached just below and several centimeters above the base of an existing Teotihuacan step but did not extend beneath it. The underlying cascajo Layer 3 deposits became thinner near the step. Figure 7.4 distinguishes a modern packed dirt surface (Layer 1), a Teotihuacan concrete floor (Layer 2), underlying Layer 3 deposits including a fire pit, and a lower compacted earthen floor (field Layer 3c), above lower tepetate/cascajo fill. The relationship supports construction of concrete flooring relative to the step but does not establish an exact building date.
